::: {.lead}
A player writes to the support desk of *Byte Bay*: "Pocket Quest stutters on
my PC." Another one: "Voice chat does not work on my phone." Before the team
can help, it must look into the operating system: its version, the running
processes, the free storage, the devices and the permissions. In lecture 9
you learned what the OS does. In this seminar you take a **tour** of two
operating systems, Windows on the lab computer and the OS of your own phone,
and you compare how they treat a game. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary operating-system system-settings task-manager device-driver app-permission sandbox app-storage foreground-app background-app process >}}

## 10.1 A tour of the PC: four tools of Windows

When a PC game has a problem, a developer opens four tools of Windows. Each
tool shows one service of the OS (@fig-pc).

| Tool (shortcut) | What it shows | OS service |
|---|---|---|
| Settings › System › About (Win + I) | Windows version, CPU, RAM, 64-bit | the system |
| Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) | processes, CPU %, memory, disk, GPU | processes, memory |
| File Explorer (Win + E) | drives, free space, folders | files |
| Device Manager (right-click Start) | devices and their drivers | devices |

: Four tools of Windows for a game developer. {#tbl-pc}

![The four tools of the tour, with what a developer reads in each one.](images/pc-tour.png){#fig-pc width=96%}

A **device driver** is a small program that lets the OS control one kind of
hardware, for example the graphics card or a gamepad. A missing or old
driver is a common reason why a device does not work in a game.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.1 — The game stutters"}
Omar's PC game stutters.

1. Task Manager › Processes: a video converter uses 85 % of the CPU.
2. The game gets few time slices (lecture 9), so its frames come late.
3. Omar closes the converter, and the game runs smoothly again.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.2 — The gamepad does not work"}
Ali's new gamepad does nothing in the game.

1. Device Manager › "Human Interface Devices" shows the gamepad with a
   yellow warning sign.
2. The sign means that Windows has no working driver for it.
3. Ali installs the driver from the maker, and the gamepad works.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Restarting the game again and again. First look: Task Manager shows what
uses the CPU and the RAM, and Device Manager shows if a device has a
problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Four facts about the lab computer"}
Use the four tools of @tbl-pc.

1. Write the Windows version and the RAM (About).
2. Write the process with the most CPU now (Task Manager).
3. Write the free space of drive C: (File Explorer).
4. Write the name of the graphics card (Device Manager › Display adapters).

*Your result:* four facts, each with the tool you used.
:::

## 10.2 A tour of the phone: Settings

A phone has no Task Manager for the player. Its OS shows the same services
in the **Settings** app (@fig-phone). Android and iOS use different names,
and phone makers change the menus a little, but four places are always
there.

| Place in Settings | What it shows |
|---|---|
| About phone (iPhone: General › About) | OS version, model, storage (and RAM on Android) |
| Battery | how much of the battery each app used |
| Storage (iPhone: General › iPhone Storage) | free space, and the space of each app |
| Apps › a game (iPhone: Settings › the game) | its permissions; on Android also Force stop and Clear cache |

: Four places in the Settings of a phone. {#tbl-phone}

![Four screens of the phone's Settings that a game developer uses.](images/phone-tour.png){#fig-phone width=96%}

A mobile OS runs each app in its own **sandbox**: the app has its own
folder and its own memory, and it cannot read the files of other apps. To use
the camera, the microphone or the location, it needs an **app permission**
from the player.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.3 — The storage of Pocket Quest"}
Settings › Apps › Pocket Quest › Storage shows 3.2 GB:

1. the app itself: 2.1 GB;
2. the user data (progress, downloaded levels): 0.9 GB;
3. the cache: 0.2 GB. "Clear cache" frees it; the game makes it again
   (lecture 4).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.4 — Voice chat is silent"}
Lina's voice chat does not work.

1. Settings › Apps › Pocket Quest › Permissions: Microphone is "Not
   allowed".
2. The OS does not give the game the microphone, so the game hears nothing.
3. Lina allows the microphone, and voice chat works.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Clearing the **storage** (or "data") of a game to free space. This deletes
the user data too: the player may lose the progress. Clear the **cache**
first.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/settings-explorer.html" poster="sims/settings-explorer.png" title="Settings Explorer: find the answer in a phone's Settings" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The tour of your phone"}
On your own phone, open Settings (or first try **Settings Explorer** above).

1. Write the OS version.
2. Choose a game or another big app: write its storage and its permissions.
3. Write the app that used the most battery today.

*Your result:* the OS version, one app with its storage and permissions, and
the battery leader.
:::

## 10.3 The same game on a PC and on a phone

*Byte Bay* sells Pocket Quest for Windows and for phones. The game code is
almost the same, but the two operating systems treat it differently
(@fig-compare). The team must plan for both.

![How Windows and a phone OS treat the same game.](images/pc-vs-mobile.png){#fig-compare width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.5 — A call during a match"}
1. **Phone:** a call arrives. The OS shows the call screen, and the game goes
   to the background. The OS pauses it, and may close it if the RAM is
   needed (lecture 9). The game must pause the match and save.
2. **PC:** the player presses Alt + Tab to answer a message. The game keeps
   running in the background, and an online match goes on.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.6 — Installing and files"}
1. **Phone:** the player installs the game from the app store (on Android
   also from an APK file). The game can only see its own sandbox folder.
2. **PC:** the player installs from a store or with an installer program.
   The game can usually read and write in many folders, for example
   Documents.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing the mobile version like a PC game. On a phone, test what happens when
a call arrives, when the player switches apps, and when the player refuses a
permission.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · PC or phone?"}
Start a game (or a video) on your phone and on the lab computer. Switch to
another app for one minute, then come back.

1. What did the game do on each device: did it keep running, pause or start
   again?
2. Write one more difference between the two operating systems from
   @fig-compare that you can see yourself.

*Your result:* two observations and one difference.
:::

## Case study: the support desk of Byte Bay

On Monday morning the support desk of *Byte Bay* gets six tickets about
*Pocket Quest*: Lina's voice chat says "Microphone not allowed" (phone);
Omar's game stutters (Windows PC); Sara's update fails with "Not enough
space" (phone); Ali's new gamepad does not work (Windows PC); Maya asks if
her phone has Android 12 or newer, which the game needs; and Yousef's phone
is empty after one hour of play. For each ticket, the team must send the
player to the right place of the OS. The Game challenge of the interactive
lesson uses these tickets. In the mini-game below you answer them.

{{< sim file="sims/help-ticket.html" poster="sims/help-ticket.png" title="Help Ticket: send each player to the right place of the OS" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Microsoft Support, "Task Manager" and "Update drivers in Windows". Android
Help, "Change app permissions on your Android phone"; Apple Support, "Control
access to hardware features" (iPhone). Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne,
*Operating System Concepts*, 10th ed., Chapter 2 (operating-system services).

## Exercises

1. Which Windows tool shows the processes and their CPU use? How do you open
   it?
2. Where do you find the Windows version and the RAM of a PC?
3. What is a device driver? Give a game example.
4. Where does a phone show which app used the most battery?
5. Pocket Quest takes 3.2 GB: app 2.1 GB, user data 0.9 GB, cache 0.2 GB.
   What does "Clear cache" free? What would "Clear storage" delete?
6. What is a sandbox? Why can a mobile game not read the photos of the
   gallery app without permission?
7. A call arrives during a mobile match. What does the OS do with the game?
8. Give two differences between Windows and a phone OS for a game.
9. *Byte Bay*: Maya asks if her phone can install the game. Where does she
   look?
10. *Byte Bay*: Yousef's phone is empty after one hour of play. Where does he
    look, and what does he find there?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Task Manager; Ctrl + Shift + Esc.
2. Settings › System › About.
3. A small program that lets the OS control one kind of hardware, for example the driver of a gamepad or a graphics card.
4. Settings › Battery.
5. 0.2 GB of temporary files; Clear storage would also delete the user data (0.9 GB of progress and downloads).
6. A closed area of storage and memory for each app; the OS keeps apps apart, so the game needs the player's permission.
7. It shows the call screen, moves the game to the background and pauses it; it may close it if the RAM is needed.
8. For example: background (keeps running or paused), memory full (page file or closing apps), files (many folders or sandbox), permissions, input.
9. Settings › About phone: the Android version.
10. Settings › Battery: how much of the battery each app used (for example Pocket Quest 34 %).
:::
